utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, good afternoon to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you and good afternoon to you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours and good afternoon to Defence counsel. I'm Patricia Sellers from the Office of the Prosecutor. With me is co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, we represent Mr. Naser Oric. We are accompanied by our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: None from the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's bring in the witness, please. Have you come to an agreement between you? I mean, Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Roberts, or Madam Vidovic, who is going to be in charge? You. Are you come to an agreement that you will limit it and finish today? MR. DI FAZIO: For my part, and I understand the Defence also cooperating in this, we're going to endeavour to finish this witness today. I've pared my in chief down and it's going to be fairly -- fairly skeleton-like, a rough outline and of a system that existed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: -- and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon to you, Mr. Eric. I want to make sure, and you seem that -- it seems that there are no problems. I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to make sure that the sound level in your headphones is correct; in other words, it's not too loud or too low.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the interpreters heard what you said. Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You have been a Judge in your own country, so you know more or less what the procedure is. Before you start giving evidence, we have -- we are bound by our Rules to administer a solemn declaration to each and every witness. The solemn declaration is to the effect that you will be testifying the truth and it is contained in the piece of paper you've just been handed. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Could you please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, Mr. Eric, I want to put some personal details to you. All I require is that you agree with me if they're correct; if not, point it out. You're of Serb ethnicity. You're currently retired. You were born in Zvornik in the village of Celopek in -- on the 8th of November, 1946. Your father's name is Vasilije. You're married. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As far as your education is concerned, you attended at Sarajevo University between 1965 and 1970 where you obtained a degree in law. Between April and September of 1970, you worked as a legal clerk in the Zvornik municipality where you conducted what can be broadly described as legal aid-type work.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You performed your military service between September 1970 and August 1971, whereupon you returned to the Zvornik municipality, continued your legal work until about May of 1973. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Between May of 1973 and August of 1980, you were the secretary at the medical centre in Zvornik. However, the work that you performed there was work of a legal nature and also involved the drafting of regulations. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: During the 1970s, you completed two exams as part of your continuing legal education. Firstly, you completed what's essentially a bar exam, referred to as the examine for the Secretariat for Administration and the Judiciary, and that qualified you to work as an investigative judge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I passed my bar exam in 1975, not in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks very much. I'm sorry about that. But the other details are correct. I take it.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, you passed another exam, referred to as a "state exam," the effect of which permitted you to work within state institutions, for example, postings in the municipalities that existed throughout the former Bosnia. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In September of 1980, you were appointed as a judge of the Zvornik Municipal Court where you worked for a number of years, and in October of 1987, you were appointed as president of the Municipal Court in Zvornik, and you continued to hold that position until you -- until your retirement in February 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As a result of those studies, those exams, and that work experience, have you become familiar with the procedures and laws applying to courts in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with the operation of municipal courts in particular throughout -- as they worked throughout Bosnia in the period of time leading up to the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber some details of the court structure, basic details of the court structure as it existed in Bosnia prior -- in the period of time leading up to the outbreak of war. Firstly, the Municipal Court. Did every municipality have a municipal court or did it vary according to the size of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war broke out, municipal courts existed for the territory of a municipality. Mostly one court for one municipality. However, there were also some municipal courts which were founded for several municipalities. Those were municipalities that had fewer residents and smaller territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period of time leading up to the outbreak of war in 1992, did Zvornik have a municipal court, and did Srebrenica have a municipal court?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it common to refer to municipal courts from time to time as a basic court or a court of first instance?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a basic court or, as we called it, municipal court. Occasionally they were called basic courts and then the name would be changed to municipal courts, but those are the same courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And generally speaking, did the jurisdiction of basic courts or courts of first instance or municipal courts in normal and usual circumstances include jurisdiction over more minor and simple criminal matters?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war broke out, the jurisdiction of basic or municipal courts in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina covered only minor cases, whereas the district courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina dealt with more complex, more serious cases within the realm of criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following the outbreak of war in early 1992, did the jurisdiction of the Municipal Courts, at least in your area where you lived, alter in any respect?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: In May of 1992, the jurisdiction of basic courts was changed so that all cases were instituted in first instance courts, whereas the district courts or second instance courts only dealt with appeals in criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following the end of hostilities, did matters revert to their pre-war system?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned district courts. Is it the case that they were in effect the next level up from courts -- from municipal courts?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, did they deal with what might be called more serious and more complex crimes?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they also act as an appeal court from decisions of the Municipal Courts?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of war in early 1992, which -- let me withdraw that question. The geographical area covered by district courts, did it include or could it include several municipality -- several municipalities or parts of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The district courts were founded or existed for the territory covered by several basic or municipal courts, which means that as a rule, they covered several jurisdictions, several municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to the war and in normal circumstances, which District Court would have covered the area or included the area of the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: That would be the district of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And beyond the district courts, was there another level of court called the Supreme Court?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where was that court based?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: You mean before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And after the war?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: After the war, in Pale, and then later on in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did these Supreme Courts, wherever they might be based, have essentially an appellate jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, although they dealt with other cases in other fields, and they dealt with complex cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. I want to ask you now some questions -- move away from the court structure and ask you some questions regarding criminal investigations. The -- was there a role in criminal investigations for a prosecutor and investigating judge and police?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did criminal investigations from time to time result in the production of an indictment and a subsequent trial?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- sorry. And was that often accompanied by investigations conducted by police, investigating judges and prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that in the majority of cases?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In certain simple cases, cases that were not complex, factually complex or involved any complex question of law, was there ever a situation where matters proceeded to trial without an investigation?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Trial Chamber the sort of situations in which that occurred and what the procedures were? I'd like to get through this -- this section of your evidence fairly swiftly, please.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Those were the cases which were simple, minor criminal offences in which the prosecutor, without conducting an investigation, could file criminal charges before a court, based on which a trial would be instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want you to turn your attention to the other situation where criminal matters were investigated and the procedures involved in that investigation leading to the production of an indictment and eventual trial. In other words, cases where they weren't simple or -- or -- or not -- complex, complex cases, in other words. Following the commission of a crime, would the police go out and gather evidence and material to assist in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would the evidence and material that they gather include reports on interviews with suspects and witnesses?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would include interviews with suspects and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Once that mass of material had been gathered, what did the police do with that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: After all of that was gathered, the police would write criminal complaints against certain suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What would they do with that criminal complaint?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The police would forward criminal complaints to the prosecutor who would have jurisdiction for those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Once the prosecutor had received the criminal complaint, was he empowered to require additional investigation -- was he empowered to acquire additional investigation?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was empowered to request additional information from the police or evidence if he or she believed them to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage of the matter, was a prosecutor entitled to disregard or dismiss the criminal complaint if the prosecutor considered the evidence was insufficient to warrant a charge or warrant a trial or warrant further action?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was empowered to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. If the prosecutor considered that there was sufficient evidence to carry on with the matter, would the prosecutor then create a document called a request for conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What would the prosecutor do with that particular document?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor would take this request for conducting an investigation and forward it to the court with jurisdiction over the matter. If this was the basic public prosecutor, then it would have been the same as the basic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the -- and is it the case that the matter would then go to -- fall into the hands of an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- this document that you have referred to, the request for conducting investigation, did it contain information such as a suspect's name, background information about a suspect, the reasons for any suspicion, suggestions for types of further investigation that might be conducted, suggestions for witnesses who might be interviewed, suggestions for the sort of evidence that ought to be gathered, and suggestions as to whether or not arrests should be made or not?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Once the matter had reached the court and the investigating judge, was a file created in the court?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did that have a C, C for Charlie, I for igloo, CI number called a "krivicni istrazni"?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you mean. That kind of a file would normally be marked as "KI," which means criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was the investigating judge empowered at this stage of the matter to dismiss the matter entirely if he or she thought that the evidence was insufficient or did not merit further action?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: After receiving a file, the investigating judge was at liberty to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disagree with the investigation and forward the case to a chamber. These cases, however, were extremely rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about the more common situation. Once having received the request for conducting investigation and getting the file number attached to a particular case, did the investigating judge in the Municipal Court have power to summons a suspect for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did that commonly occur?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: This always occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And would -- thank you. And would the investigating judge then interrogate the suspect and would a record be taken of that interrogation, either minutes or transcript or some sort of record of what the suspect said?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Minutes would be taken of the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Following the -- immediately following the interrogation and the taking of minutes, what was the next step in this procedure?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge would then pass a decision to adopt the prosecutor's request and open an investigation against the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Against the suspect." Interpreter's correction. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. And at this stage, is this decision put in writing?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is this commonly known as the decision to conduct an investigation or "resenje"?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Decision to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at this document that I produce to you. Okay. Now that you've got your spectacles on, could you cast your eye over the document and tell us if this is an example of just such a decision that you have told us about, a decision to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And obviously it's plain, isn't it, that one of the subjects of investigation is the defendant in this case? I'll return to that later, but firstly I want to ask you about some features of this document. Firstly, you signed the document? If you go to the back, I think you'll find a signature there.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you go to the beginning of the document, you see in the top left corner a number, Ki-81/93. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is this the file number that you talked about moments ago in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: That is indeed the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in the first one or two or three lines of the document, it says -- it refers to you "deciding upon a request submitted by the municipal public prosecutor in Zvornik." Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've described to the Trial Chamber the procedures. The police going out, getting evidence, making a criminal complaint, sending it on to the prosecutor, his evaluation, and then the prosecutors forwarding it on to the court. Is that what that reference to a decision on the request submitted by the municipal public prosecutor is talking about? All of those processes had occurred?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, the police file a criminal complaint, then the prosecutor files a request to conduct an investigation. And then what comes next is a decision like this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. And now go to the last page of the document where your signature is. Your signature is preceded by a part of the document that is headed "Explanation." There there is a reference to this history of the prosecutor submitting to the court the request to conduct an investigation against the accused Naser Oric. You've told us about that. And then it refers to a proposal that the accused be taken into custody due to their having committed a war crime against the civilian population under Article 142 of the Republika Srpska Criminal Code. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if it was normal or common or whether it happened from time to time that the prosecutor would propose, when he's forwarding the request to conduct an investigation, would propose that a certain person and an accused be taken into custody? Would that happen very often?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: It would happen sometimes that the prosecutor proposed that a person should be detained. In this specific case, that was precisely what the prosecutor proposed. Otherwise, this option would not have been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So it could occur that there would be a proposal to arrest or, rather, take an accused into custody, or there might not be, and that depended on the prosecutor. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There is a reference to an Article 142 of the Republika Srpska Criminal Code. Was that, as far as you are aware, a new offence that had come into being after the outbreak of war, or as far as you're aware, had it existed for some time prior to the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Okay. Let him answer the question first and then maybe I make the comment later. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Article 142? Was that a fresh or recent charge, or was it -- had it existed prior to the outbreak of war in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: It existed prior to the outbreak of war in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When was Republika Srpska created? Mr. Eric perhaps knows the answer. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know the answer off the top of my head, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When was Republika Srpska proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe in January 1992, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go ahead anyway. I'm not -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a question with regard to the criminal code of Republika Srpska. Was this a completely new code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, this is why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Or was it taken either from Bosnia-Herzegovina or was it taken from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not new in its entirety. The code was adopted from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the special provisions, and the general provisions from the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And this may be an element of repetition, but as far as the laws relating to procedure -- criminal procedure, the gathering of evidence and types of criminal charges, did the Republika Srpska adopt the body of law that existed prior to the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened? Was fresh legislation enacted, or did it adopt the existing legislation? That's what I want to know, as far as criminal procedure, and criminal evidence, criminal trials and jurisdictions of courts and so on.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No, there was no fresh legislation. The existing criminal legislation was adopted. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Police prior to the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you following up on the previous topic or not? Because it's still a little bit hazy. I mean, so far we know that as far as the general part of criminal law, they derived the code of Republika Srpska from the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia the special -- you know, in continental systems, criminal law is divided into three, the general part, the special part, and procedural part. We've dealt with the general. We've dealt with the special. The special came from Bosnia. But we still don't have a clear answer where the procedural part of the code of Republika Srpska came from. First we had an answer which is "no, it did not come from anywhere," and then we had an answer that it did come from somewhere because there wasn't anything new, but we still don't know where it came from. I know from other cases, but basically I have to shut down what I know. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've told us that -- you've told us that there was no fresh legislation following the outbreak of war and that existing criminal legislation was adopted. What I want to know is this: The body of law dealing with criminal offences, the procedure for criminal offends, how to deal with them, issues of jurisdiction for criminal offences, the duties of judges to apply that criminal procedure, did the body of law applicable to that change or alter following the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This may be confusing to the witness, because questions of jurisdiction under European continental criminal law fall within the general part of criminal law and not under procedure as such. So -- not necessarily, but, say in Italy and France they certainly do. But I'm not quite sure that it was the same in Yugoslavia. So he needs to -- you need to enlighten us on this, Mr. Eric, because you are the one who is best positioned to do that in this courtroom. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: My question is: The body of law relating to criminal procedure, how to deal with crimes, did that alter in Bosnia, in the Republika Srpska -- in the Republika Srpska following the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: After the war broke out, not a single law was changed. The criminal law, the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was applied, and the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the federal criminal law. Therefore, the legal regulations already in existence were still applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When you speak about jurisdiction, do you also speak about the organisation of the courts? Because I understood your explanation regarding jurisdiction in the way that during the war the jurisdiction changed between the municipal court and the district court, so that the municipal court got a wider jurisdiction than you had had before the war in that it was changed again after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The jurisdiction of courts in general was enshrined in a special enactment called Law On Regular Courts. Jurisdiction was altered in May 1992. Since that change the municipal courts have jurisdiction over all criminal cases. Once the war was over, this same law was again amended and jurisdiction was distributed or divided between the basic courts and the municipal and district courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Sorry. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were police officers obliged to enforce the laws relating to criminal procedure both prior to and after the war?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were obliged to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did that oblige them to act upon complaints and investigate criminal conduct both prior to and after the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that definitely obliged them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Going back to the document that you have in front of you. The subject of this particular decision to investigate is Mr. Naser Oric. Apart from the particular decision to investigate that you have before you, did you sign and issue other decisions to conduct investigations where Mr. Oric was the -- was the subject or one of the subjects of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: There were other such decisions, all of them pursuant to requests by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever initiate an investigation by yourself or acting alone against Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P492.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and admitted and marked as Prosecutor Exhibit P492. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It's more a question of language. At the end of the English translation, the document reads: "The appeal is filed to this court's trial chamber." Does this mean that an appeal has been filed, or if one is filed that it has to go to the trial chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It has to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It has to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words -- this is common because I have to deal with such documents in other cases. Basically it states that there is a time limit for the filing of the appeal and the filing has to go through the trial chamber -- it has to be filed in the registry on the trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It has to be filed instead of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Should I clarify that with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is basically what it says. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll ask the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You may have heard that exchange, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can look at the last line, actually. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Look at the last line of P492, and tell us the significance of that particular proviso.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read -- can you read that last line aloud, please, so that we have it translated, and then could you explain what the procedure would be if one wished to lodge an appeal against such a decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Information about appeals. In decision may be appealed within three days from the delivery of the decision. The appeal shall be forwarded to the criminal chamber of this court." This means that this decision may be appealed in accordance with the legislation and that this appeal ought to be sent to the criminal chamber of this same court, which comprises three professional judges who will decide on the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I think that satisfies Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to right now wrap up this issue of the broad outline of criminal investigations. Following the issuance of your decision to conduct an investigation, is there a -- is that followed by an investigative hearing which is scheduled by the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At that hearing are witnesses questioned, interrogated, and minutes and a record created of what's said?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that hearing, the evidence that had been proposed would be adduced. That would be done by the prosecutor. And that included the examination of witnesses whose names had been previously proposed or suggested, and their statements would be recorded in minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And does the investigative judge have the power to call witnesses independently, other witnesses of that not been proposed by the prosecutor? In other words, to make his own decision about some witnesses that should or should not be called -- should be called?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. The investigative judge did have the power to call witnesses who perhaps were proposed by the suspect or to call witnesses who in view of the investigative judge ought to be examined or interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Once this mass of material has been gathered together, what is done with it?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: When this material has been gathered, the investigative judge would make a finding declaring the investigation concluded, and in a separate letter would state this finding and forward the entire file to the prosecutor for him to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Once the prosecutor has received this material, I want to know what his options are, his or her options are. Can the prosecutor return the matter to the court and the investigative judge for further investigation? Is that an option?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was also possible. He could have returned the file to the investigative judge in order for the investigation to be supplemented by certain measures, and those measures would be indicated in a written proposal. It would be stated what else the investigative judge needs to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the -- does the prosecutor have the option of not proceeding any further with the matter if he or she considers that the evidence is insufficient?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. The prosecutor could discontinue or decide not to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And finally, does the prosecutor have the option of writing or issuing an indictment against a suspect or suspects?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If that last option occurs, the prosecutor decides to issue an indictment and proceed, does the matter then proceed to trial?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you summarise the steps that are taken from that point onwards to the point where trial is commenced?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The file would be sent to the office of the clerk of the court, would receive an identification which would be K, meaning that it was a criminal case, and then depending on what else was on the docket, the case would be assigned to the judge who would then make preparations for a trial, that is to say send the indictment to all the parties to see whether any of them would file a motion objecting to certain aspects of the indictment, and following that a trial would be scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move from -- to another topic at this juncture. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P386. Sorry. Perhaps before that occurs, I omitted to tender or produce to the Trial Chamber the English translations of this exhibit, which are overdue and now have to be put before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it already, but I suppose we can use this just to make sure that we are using the same document that you have or that you are circulating now. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. Do Your Honours already have a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I didn't realise. I was informed that you didn't have a translation. But if that's the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We already have it marked as P386E. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to Your Honours. I'll just ask that it be handed back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just before I move on to this topic, Witness, there is one other question I want to ask you. During the course of the war or indeed after, did you ever have an opportunity to interrogate or ask questions of Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you know him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Now, look at the statements, please. You have Exhibit P386 before you, and I think I can lead you through this evidence. It's uncontroversial. They consist -- the exhibit exists of a number of statements by a number of different individuals. What I would like you to do is to flick through them and tell the Trial Chamber if your signature appears at the end of each of those statements.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. They all appear to be, apart from the main body of the text, a pro forma document, "Minutes Of The Testimony Of Witness".

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber at what point in a criminal investigation such documents might be created?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: A document such as this one may be drafted before an investigation is initiated, before criminal proceedings are instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If, as you say, such a document could be drawn up before -- even before an investigation has been authorised or commenced, on whose initiative would such a document be drawn? Who would take the initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This particular document or these documents that have been presented to me have not been drawn up by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, because we need to understand: When you say these documents could be drawn before -- drawn up before an investigation has even started, is it because something -- did I read you correctly? And if such a document may be drafted before an investigation is initiated, would it be procedurally correct or would it be an abuse of power to draft or to draw up such a statement? Who would -- who would be able to authorise the drawing up -- the taking of such a statement and the drawing up of such a statement if there is no investigation in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the so-called additional criminal investigative steps, and it was possible to take a statement from certain persons before criminal proceedings were instituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But who would take them, and on which -- on which or on whose authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would be done by a judge. If you mean this specific case, I can explain to you how this was created, how this came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can -- we will definitely need to come to that, but before we come to that, if there is no investigation yet started, initiated, how does the judge come to interview or interrogate a person and draw up such a statement? How does the judge fit in this process if there is no investigation yet in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the investigation has not been initiated yet, then the judge would avail himself of this possibility to take a statement from a person pertaining to an event or an act that had been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, I'm not going to ask him the other question that relates to this particular document which he seemed to be offering to give us information about or to answer. That's your -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's what I'm going to proceed to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at the statements that are before you, they obviously have on the pro forma first page a section that specifies that there are criminal proceedings against, and a blank space. And presumably normally the suspect's or the defendant's name would be included in that particular blank space. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No. This is a form, a pre-printed form. So that does not have to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It may not have to be the case -- I'll withdraw that. In normal circumstances, would you expect the name of the person to be inserted there?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the proceedings had been initiated, then yes, the name of the person would be inserted here. But in this case no proceedings had been initiated before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get to that in due course. I'm going to get to that in due course, but I'm just asking you about what would normally happen. And again there's a space obviously specifying the particular article that has been breached, article whatever from the penal code. In normal circumstances, would you expect the particular article to be inserted there?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: A very specific question of verification, because it may have to do with the translation. Now, when you speak of investigation and criminal proceeding, is it the same or are these two different phases of some sort of finding evidence, because in some countries you indeed have -- you indeed distinguish between investigation, which may not be called criminal proceeding. Now, is this the case or has this been the case in your country? So my main question is: Investigation and criminal proceeding, is it the same or is there some difference between these two terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of that falls under criminal proceedings. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me deal with this series of documents in this way: Do you know a gentleman named Pavle Jelisavcic, or have you met a gentleman named Pavle Jelisavcic?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did -- when did he -- when did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: That happened in 1994, in mid-1994, or perhaps a bit later. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And where did you meet him, and how did you come to meet him?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: He came to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself and explained that he was from the committee for gathering information about war crimes in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did he explain to you what his purpose was, why he wanted to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was -- what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: He told me that the committee and the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska had an arrangement whereby representatives of the committee were authorised to take statements in the field from citizens regarding certain events, and this is what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours, please. It's almost time for the break. It's -- this would be for my purposes a good time. Could we have the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Di Fazio. Yes. Before we break, Judge Brydensholt has got one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When you were told there was this arrangement regarding taking explanations from witnesses in the field, were you shown any documents, any authorisation or anything, or was it just oral you were told that he had such an authorisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He just told me that verbally. Yes. I only received verbal information. I did not see anything in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Brydensholt. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You told us just prior to the -- to the break of the visit of Mr. Pavle -- I forget his surname, the gentleman who came to visit you from the committee in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Jelisavcic. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Jelisavcic. And he was informing you that there was an arrangements between the Ministry of Justice of the Republika Srpska and the committee whereby the committee members or representatives would go and take statements in the field. You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he tell you what precisely he was going to do?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: He said that he would be taking statements on the spot regarding events that occurred in the villages around Srebrenica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he say for what purpose these statements were going to be taken?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What particular assistance did he seek from you?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Once he was back from the field, he asked me to process those statements, to sign them, to have them photocopied. He then took the copies and left the original statements with the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he tell you of this -- that that was his plan prior to going out in the field and taking the statements or did he say that only upon his return?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: He said so prior to going out to take statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that? How did you -- what did you think of that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: At the time, my reaction was to phone the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska. I spoke to the then-deputy or assistant minister, Goran Neskovic. I told him about Pavle's visit. He confirmed that there was indeed such an agreement and that Pavle was authorised to take statements, after which I agreed to go along with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So did Pavle then go out into the field and carry out his work and come back eventually with the statements?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pavle went out with his own recording clerk and driver, in his own vehicle. He was away for a while, and when he was back, he brought the records or statements that I then signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he go out and take statements on only one occasion or did he go out on these field trips on -- more than once?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: He went several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit P386 that you should have before you, the B/C/S versions, look at the dates of the -- the ostensible dates of the statements, and they're on the -- at the front of each statement, and they cover dates such as the 27th of August, 1994, in the case of Ratko Nikovic; 25th of August, 1994, in the case of Nedeljko Radic; 24th of August, 1994, in the case of Slavoljub Zikic; 16th of September, 1994, in the case of Ilija Ivanovic; and 25th of August, 1994, in the case of Veselin Sarac. Do you see those dates?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What do those dates represent as far as you're aware, the date that the statement was apparently taken from the person, or the date upon which you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The date the statements were taken. I signed the statements once Pavle was back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There's just some features about the statements that I want to draw your attention to. If you look at the bottom near your signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to, because there is his signature allegedly on each page dated 19th of August, 2004, and he can explain why it appears on these documents and why that date in particular. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is his signature at the end of each statement. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. I want to cover precisely those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: An all encompassing question. It covers all of these statements. You see your signature at the bottom of each page and at the end of the statements, and at the bottom of the signature -- at the bottom of the page where your signature appears, there's the date that appears there to be 19th of August, 2004, and of course that predates the ostensible date upon which the statement was taken. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I signed these documents only on the last page when Pavle Jelisavcic brought me these documents to sign. As for these signatures dated the 19th of August, 2004, 1994 relate to the date when I signed the statements in the presence of the investigators of this International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So when did you in fact append your signature to these documents in 1994, when Pavle brought them back or at some other time? When he brought them back and they were completed?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of August, 2004, the investigators requested me to sign each page of the document. The time when I only signed the last page, it was in the same form as now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I want to know. When did you sign the last page? Was it prior to Pavle going out and taking the statements or was it when he brought them back to you completed?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: When he brought them back to me completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio. I hate to interrupt you like this, but something that has been going around and around and around in my head and I need some kind of an explanation from the witness in order to have it click. In the Zvornik Municipal Court, how many judges were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean at the time these statements were taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember for sure, but we must have been six or seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that at the time, you were already appointed as president of the Zvornik Municipal Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As president of the Zvornik Municipal Court, would it have been your task to act as an investigating judge or would that work of investigating judge be done by the other judges or by some of the other judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to regulations, when you have a court with few judges, the court president, too, has the task to perform different tasks and activities that are enshrined in the norms governing the work of a judge. That is why I, too, performed certain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tasks in view of these very regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware if any of the other judges that were serving in the Zvornik Municipal Court were asked to sign similar statements by this Mr. Pavle Jelisavcic, or anyone else for that matter, representing the committee for collecting information on war criminals -- on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He came to see me in my official capacity as the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're not aware that other judges of your court or from your court had been approached by him or by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Didn't you find it strange to say the least that out of all the judges he would pick on the most important, hierarchically, of the court itself to sign statements which under normal circumstances would be signed by junior judges or investigative judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When someone addresses a court, the first person to address is usually the president, and that's why Pavle picked me. He explained why he was there. He introduced himself. Then I consulted with the Ministry of Justice and subsequently the statements that I signed were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let's go on. Let's proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the context of your work, in the pre-war years and in the war years from 1992 up until late 1994, about the time these statements were taken, had you ever met with such a request before?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is what you did -- sorry, the request that you entertained and the subsequent inquiries that you made with the Ministry of Justice a wholly unusual matter for you?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the top of any one of these statements. Say, for example, look at the top of the statement of Ratko Nikolic. That's -- do you have that? Yes. It's 03602046. You see that number at the top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. In fact, you may be able to see it on the screen in front of you as well if you wish. No. I take it that back. It's not up on the screen. Okay. It's got a number there. You see? Kri 77/, what I think is 94. What does that number represent?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction here. It's Kry -- Kri 77/94.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. But there are obviously numbers and different numbers but they appear on these statements at the top in the same location. All right? With -- perhaps I'd better do this individually. I'll withdraw my question and let's start -- if I might have the assistance of the usher. I'd like you to look at the statement of Ratko Nikolic, please. Now that's got a number at the top right-hand corner, 77/94. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And if you take a look at the statement of Mr. Nadeljko Radic, you see the number there is Kri 73/94. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are all different numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. I just want to take you through -- through them just to be absolutely certain about all of this, okay? And if you look at the statement of Slavoljub Zikic, you see that the lettering and numbering there is Kri 68/94.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And if you look at the statement of Ilija Ivanovic, that has no Kri and merely has 94/94. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: And there must be another Kri here, it's just that it's not quite clear or maybe they failed to write it, but it must be. There must be another Kri marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And finally for the sake of completeness, the statement of Veselin Sarac, that bears the endorsement in the same place, Kri-74/94. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber what those numbers represent?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: These letters and numbers represent the case number in the file of criminal offences. Therefore, these recorded interviews were processed, entered into these files, and these are the file numbers attached to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whose files? Whose files? Who -- I take it that you're telling us that you had absolutely nothing to do with the drawing up of these statements except that you accepted to sign at the end of each one of them. But I also take it, therefore, that the insertion of the reference number is not your own work. Someone else inserted that. I take it that this Mr. -- whatever his name is. MR. DI FAZIO: Pavle Jelisavcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pavle Jelisavcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only signed these. After I signed the statements, the recording clerks entered them into their respective files and assigned them numbers. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But why -- why did they do that? Were they taken in relation too -- let me withdraw that and let me approach it this way: These different numbers -- you can tell me if I'm right or wrong. These numbers that you have at the top left-hand corner, do they all represent different investigations into different people, different incidents?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each statement is processed and entered separately and given a different number in order to leave some sort of a paper trail that can later be traced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So was this Mr. Pavle Jelisavcic going out and taking statements in respect of the different cases represented by these different numbers? Is that what you understood or was that not your understanding?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Pavle Jelisavcic took all these statements that I have in front of me now, and these statements were duly processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Look at this first statement, the one of Ratko Nikolic which you have in front of you or you had in front of you a couple of minutes ago. Look at the first page. It doesn't bear a number. But if you look at the second page, at the very top right-hand corner you see STR Strana 2. So I take it that this Pavle, when coming to your office, would come with this statement of Ratko Nikolic, which would include also the first page, wouldn't it? In other words, he would come with the statement ready with the first page that I am showing you here. The first page would not be compiled or drawn up by your clerks but by Mr. Pavle himself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In practice, you never put a number on the first page. What I see here is the first page, but it was not given a number, an ordinal number, because that is not the established practice. You start with page 2 and then mark the document throughout, except for the first page, the cover page, which remains unmarked with the exception of this number that we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the first page is signed by Ratko Nikolic as well. The first page is signed by Ratko Nikolic. That's why I put it to you that he -- this Mr. Pavle must have brought the entire statement including page number 1. And what I am asking you, did your office then insert on that page Kri 77/94, or did Pavle bring it to you with that reference number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavle did not bring this page with the number. It was our office that marked the numbers, this number, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What that's that VE/NB-1 at the top right hand, handwritten next to the reference number? VE, I take it, Vaso Eric. NB. I don't know if it's Nebojsa or not but it may be your office. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't want to stand here and give evidence but I suspect it's our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. MR. DI FAZIO: Because they've got -- they've got different NB 3, 4 and so on throughout the series. So I'll ask the witness just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's there on the document so we need to know. And the others are marked similarly, 1, 2, 3, 4. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. The statements all bear the handwriting VE/NB and then number a, 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. Do you recognise those numbers or has that been added to the document at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No. I don't recognise these numbers. They must have been added later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. One thing I want to know, if you can offer any assistance to us is this: These numbers at the top, and they relate to different cases, why were they given those numbers for these different cases if this guy Pavle Jelisavcic is out gathering statements on behalf of this committee in Belgrade? Why those particular action numbers or court numbers or file numbers? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: These numbers have one purpose only. It is for these statements to be quickly traceable in the court's archive. They have no other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And following the return of Pavle Jelisavcic, what happened to the originals of the statements?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: The originals were kept by the court. Pavle Jelisavcic took copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio. Again my apologies for interrupting you. Did you at any time ask Mr. Pavle Jelisavcic whether there was any tape recording of these interviews or did you just ask him any question at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't ask him any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the -- there's names of clerks that appear, court clerks, that appear on the statements. You'll see there's some names that appear from -- quite often. Gorica Trajkovic is -- appears in Ratko Nikolic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cut it short. He appears in all of them except one on which Ruzica Jaic appears. MR. DI FAZIO: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So there you have it, those two names. Are they court clerks? Were they really court clerks. Were employed by the court or were they not employees of the Municipal Court?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No. They were not employees of the Municipal Court. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have just one question before I pass you over to Madam Vidovic. Did your law require when an investigating judge is taking a statement, did the law require that a clerk also be present when the statement was being taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have no idea who Gorica Trajkovic is? Never heard the name before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was a clerk who arrived with Pavle Jelisavcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She came with him from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same as regards the other, this Jaic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She's not an official of the Municipal Court in Zvornik, but I can't really say who her employer is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you notice on this statement of Ilija Ivanovic, which mentions also her name, she is mentioned as a -- at least in the English text I have in the first page -- on the last page you have her as recording secretary, recording secretary. What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that Pavle Jelisavcic dictated the statement and she wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And you don't know whether she was a court clerk? You don't know her? You don't know the person, do you? I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. She was not with the Zvornik court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I thank you. Madam Vidovic, now, who is lead counsel for Naser Oric will be cross-examining you. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Eric. We haven't got much time left, so therefore I will ask you to be as brief whenever possible and give us yes or no answers whenever possible. Before the war, municipal courts did not have jurisdiction over serious criminal offences including murder and war crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, municipal courts in Zvornik did not have jurisdiction in cases for Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Skelani municipalities or cases from these municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that in the beginning of the war, Republika Srpska adopted a decision to expand the jurisdiction of that court, the court in Zvornik, to include the territory of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Skelani under their jurisdiction as well as to expand subject matter jurisdiction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened in May and June of that year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Such a decision could not have been forwarded to the Muslim authorities in Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At around the 8th of April, 1992, intense combat activity developed in that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Moreover, in the course of April and May 1992, Muslim population residing in Zvornik and Bratunac was driven out as well as in Skelani and the entire Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims residing in Srebrenica, Skelani, and Bratunac, including those who had fled to Srebrenica, after that area once again came under the Muslim rule had no further contacts with the authorities in Zvornik. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. That fact is not known to me. I couldn't tell you anything about those authorities, because I was employed by the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, I will ask you the following: There was no cooperation whatsoever between police, prosecutor's office, and courts in the Serbian territory on the one hand, and on the other hand, in the Muslim and Croat territory. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the time after the expulsion of Muslims from that area, meaning starting in April and May of 1992 and throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Most likely. Most likely there was no cooperation, but I don't know. I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing I'm sure you should be certain is, since you were the president of the Zvornik Municipal Court, the territorial extent or boundaries of your jurisdiction or the jurisdiction of your court. How could you not know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about the territorial jurisdiction of the court in Zvornik. It covered Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Skelani municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that was before the war broke out, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was after the war broke out. Before the war broke out, Zvornik -- the court in Zvornik had territorial jurisdiction only over Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Madam Vidovic, between the two of you, you know the position better than we do, but I want a clarification on this. Do I take it, therefore, that on paper, that is legally, the Zvornik Municipal Court still maintained jurisdiction over areas like Srebrenica, et cetera, but in practice it meant nothing or it couldn't be exercised over those territories because those territories had passed on under municipal -- under Muslim control. Is that the correct position or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what is the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like this: Srebrenica municipality has a court now, and the basic court does not have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. jurisdiction any longer over that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm speaking of April and May 1992, not now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the jurisdiction had changed in May or June of 1992. Prior to that time, basic court in Zvornik did not have jurisdiction over the territory of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move forward, Madam Vidovic, please, and my apologies to you for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it, and that's what is reflected in the transcript, that the court in Zvornik, after the war that the court in Zvornik, after the war broke out, was given jurisdiction over the territory of municipalities Skelani, Bratunac, and Srebrenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I said that the jurisdiction of the basic court in Zvornik was expanded to include the territories of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Skelani municipalities and that that was done in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, are you claiming that it was expected that the Muslim side would send criminal cases to the prosecutor and the court in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: After the jurisdiction was expanded to include those municipalities, the prosecutor could only send those cases to the court in Zvornik, because that was the only court which had jurisdiction for that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you the following: Mr. Eric, you as a judge of the court in Zvornik, did you send any cases to the prosecutor on the Muslim or Croat side? Did you have any communication with them?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will ask you something else now. You have worked in the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina for many years. You are very familiar with the regulations and provisions concerning regular courts. Isn't it true that the jurisdiction of courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina was regulated by the law on regular courts by the -- adopted by the relevant state agency?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, local authorities could not have simply decided on their own that from now on our municipality would come under the jurisdiction of a court in Sarajevo and not a court in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Local authorities never made such a decision in that particular case. The decision came from the top of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, that wasn't the point of my question. My question was as follows: In accordance with the regulations, local municipal authorities before the war or during the war were never authorised to simply decide that from now on the court in Sarajevo would have jurisdiction over our municipality and not, for example, the court in Zvornik. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You do not know whether and when the decision was made to change the jurisdiction of the regular court in Zvornik for the territory of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Skelani municipalities by the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that during the war Municipal Courts, including the court in Zvornik, were given jurisdiction to investigate war crimes, you referred to the courts in Republika Srpska, not the courts in the territory under the rule of the Federation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is to say not the territory under the control of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, you do not know what regulations were applied in 1992 and 1993 by the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory beyond the control of Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: VASO ERIC
